To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the termites and mud dauber wasps of the West Africa build earths that are consumed and used for medicinal purposes by humans and other animals.

1) the earths of insects, especially termites, are widely used as food supplements, medicines and religious objects; 2) the earths are consumed and used because they are believed to have healing properties, and are used as religious objects because they are believed, by some, to have supernatural powers; and 3) the earths have a complex and dynamic relationship with the people who use them, and with other species in their environment.
the termites and mud daubers are respected for their fertility, and that this respect is reflected in the ways in which their earths are used and consumed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social and cultural dimensions of the relationship between humans, insects and earth.
the ways in which insects are understood and used by humans in West Africa, with the aim of providing new insights into the ways that humans and insects are entangled in West Africa and beyond.
the ways that humans and insects co-constitute one another in West Africa and the implications this has for our understanding of the human and the non-human.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the earth of insects is not only used for fertility and healing but also for the protection of the earth itself.

the earths of termites and mud dauber wasps are used in West Africa for their nutritional value and medicinal properties, but that these are also imbued with symbolic significance, and the insects that make them are respected as 'ancestral beings'.
the earths of termites and mud dauber wasps are used as medicines and for fertility in West Africa, and that these earths are understood as having been made and given by these insects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

termites and wasps are not simply 'pests' but also 'benefactors' of the people of West Africa, and that the insects and humans of this region are engaged in a'symbiotic' relationship that has evolved through millennia of cohabitation.
the insects, the earths they produce and the people who use them are all engaged in a dynamic process of co-production.
we are trying to understand the relationship between the earth and human fertility.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the earths of termites and mud daubers have been incorporated into the lives of humans and other animals as part of an ecology of fertility, and as such are a powerful symbol of life and death, of the earth and the cosmos.
the termites, mud daubers and their earths are understood as having the capacity to transform the human body, and to do so in ways that are understood as both 'natural' and'spiritual'.
the earths of these insects are not just consumed for their nutrients but also for their power, and that this power is intimately connected with their reproductive capacities.
